Class URI

java.lang.Object
io.github.jabrena.juno.jdk.net.URI
public final class URI extends Object
The board-side java.net.URI: the compiler reads this class as java.net.URI, so a program that calls URI.create(...) or new URI(...) against the JDK runs this code on the board.

It parses a URI reference as RFC 3986 does: an optional scheme, then either an opaque part (mailto:a@b.org) or a hierarchical one with an optional authority (//user@host:port), a path, an optional query and an optional fragment. A URI without a scheme is a relative reference, which resolve(URI) reads against a base URI. Any scheme is accepted; java.net.http only sends http and https ones.

The URI keeps its text and where each component starts and ends, so it costs the arena the text it was created from, its host and, for an http or https URI, the request target (path?query) the client sends; none of them has a length limit. The accessors copy their component when they are called. As in the JDK, the getRaw... accessors return a component as written and the others decode its %XX escapes. A runtime String holds bytes, so an escape decodes to one byte: UTF-8 stays UTF-8.

Deviations from the JDK: a malformed URI is rejected with IllegalArgumentException by new URI(...) as well as by create (the board has no URISyntaxException); a port above 65535 is rejected; resolve(URI) follows RFC 3986, so a reference that is only a query (?q) keeps the base path, where the JDK's RFC 2396 rules drop its last segment, and an absolute-path reference loses its . and .. segments, which the JDK keeps; and equals(Object) compares %XX escapes as written.

    • resolve

      public URI resolve(URI reference)
      Resolves reference against this URI as RFC 3986 section 5.2 does: an absolute reference is returned as it is; a reference with an authority keeps only this URI's scheme; any other takes this URI's scheme and authority, and its path is merged with this URI's and has its . and .. segments removed. Against an opaque base URI, the reference is returned as it is, as in the JDK.
